issues.legal_issue: Non-payment of rent under a separate furniture contract does not constitute default justifying eviction when the tenant has paid the rent fixed for the building and the building rent was not lawfully revised.
material_facts: The rent for the rented rooms had been fixed by the Rent Controller.
Furniture was supplied later under a separate contract at a separately agreed rent, which the first appellate court found was unconnected with the original tenancy.
The tenant paid the fixed rent for the rooms but did not pay the furniture rent for the months relied on for eviction.
No order of the Rent Controller revised the fair rent of the building to include the furniture rent.
issues.conclusion: The unpaid furniture rent did not constitute a ground for eviction under section 11(1)(d), and the eviction decree could not stand on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4, 5, 7 and 11(1)(d) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, default must be in payment of the rent fixed for the building. Rent cannot be increased except in accordance with the Act; an alteration to fair rent fixed by the Rent Controller requires the Controller’s approval. Unpaid rent under a later, independent furniture contract does not become rent under the original building tenancy. No earlier cases are relied on for this principle.

rule.if: eviction_suit_for_building_rent_default and rent_fixed_by_rent_controller and (later_furniture_contract_separate_from_building_tenancy and furniture_rent_unpaid) and building_rent_paid and not controller_approved_rent_revision

predicates.eviction_suit_for_building_rent_default: A landlord brings a suit seeking eviction from a rented building on the ground of rent default.
predicates.rent_fixed_by_rent_controller: The rent payable for the building was fixed by a rent-control authority.
predicates.later_furniture_contract_separate_from_b: After the building tenancy began, the landlord and tenant made a separate contract for furniture that was not part of the original tenancy.
predicates.furniture_rent_unpaid: The tenant did not pay rent due under the separate furniture contract.
predicates.building_rent_paid: The tenant paid the rent fixed for the building for the relevant period.
predicates.controller_approved_rent_revision: The rent-control authority approved a revision of the building rent to account for the later addition or improvement.

issues.definition: When a building-rent eviction suit involves unpaid rent under a separate later furniture contract, but the rent-control authority fixed the building rent, that rent was paid, and no authority-approved revision included the furniture, the furniture arrears do not justify eviction.

issues.legal_issue: A court hearing an appeal in a contested building-possession suit may make an order for deposit of rent during the appeal.
material_facts: The landlord’s suit sought recovery of possession of a building, and the tenant contested the claim for eviction.
During the appeal, the Subordinate Judge ordered the tenant to deposit rent under section 11A.
The tenant argued that an order under section 11A could be made only by the trial court.
issues.conclusion: An order under section 11A may be made at any stage of the litigation, including in appeal, because an appeal is a continuation of the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 permits an order for deposit of rent in a contested suit for possession of a building. Since an appeal is a continuation of the suit, the landlord may obtain the benefit of such an order in the appellate court as well as in the trial court. No earlier cases are relied on for this principle.

predicates.contested_building_possession_suit: A tenant contests a landlord’s suit seeking possession of a building.
predicates.matter_in_appeal: The building-possession suit is being considered by an appellate court.
predicates.landlord_seeks_rent_deposit_order: The landlord seeks an order requiring the tenant to deposit rent while the litigation is pending.

issues.definition: If a tenant contests a building-possession suit and the landlord seeks rent deposits while the suit is in appeal, the court may order those deposits during the appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A higher court should not strike out a tenant’s defence for failure to deposit rent when it overturns a favourable compliance finding without a proper inquiry into the relevant facts.
material_facts: The first appellate court found that the tenant had produced documents showing subsequent deposits in the regular way and rejected the request to strike out the defence.

The High Court reached a contrary conclusion in second appeal after considering documentary material, without a proper inquiry into the court’s deposit procedure or the delay after the money had been handed to the Nazir.
The High Court accepted that the tenant handed the money to the Nazir, but objected that the tenant had not personally deposited it; the Nazir deposited it later.
The tenant had no adequate opportunity to establish the relevant procedure and explain the delay.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in striking out the tenant’s defence on the material before it; its contrary conclusion on compliance was reached without a proper inquiry and caused prejudice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 provides for striking out a defence for non-compliance with a rent-deposit order, but that penalty is distinct from the grounds for eviction under section 11. A higher court should not displace a positive factual finding of the first appellate court on a vital matter through an inadequate inquiry that prejudices a party. Under Order 41, rules 27 and 28 of the Code of Civil Procedure, additional evidence may be received, and the court may call for further evidence so the parties have a proper opportunity to establish their positions. No earlier cases are relied on for this principle.

predicates.second_appeal_in_eviction_suit: A higher court is hearing a second appeal arising from a suit for eviction.
predicates.first_appellate_court_found_deposit_comp: The first appellate court found that the tenant had complied with the rent-deposit order.
predicates.higher_court_reversed_compliance_finding: The higher court reached a contrary conclusion on compliance without adequately investigating the circumstances of the deposit.
predicates.tenant_lacked_fair_opportunity_to_explai: The tenant did not have a proper opportunity to establish the deposit procedure or explain the delay in the money reaching the court’s account.

issues.definition: When a higher court in a second appeal overturns the first appellate court’s finding of compliance without adequate inquiry and the tenant lacked a fair opportunity to explain the deposit, the defence must not be struck out on that basis.
